strengths: Addresses an important and timely bottleneck: Feed-forward multi-view reconstruction transformers (like VGGT and π³) scale quadratically with the sequence length due to full global cross-view attention, severely limiting their scalability to large scenes.

The analysis of global attention patterns in VGGT is insightful, demonstrating that attention maps naturally concentrate on sparse geometric correspondences and highlighting the differential role of middle layers versus early/late layers.
The proposed method is completely training-free and model-agnostic, requiring no fine-tuning or architectural alterations while maintaining broad applicability to both VGGT and π³.

Crucial domain-specific adaptation: The design choice to preserve dense connectivity for special tokens (camera embeddings and register tokens) while only sparsifying patch-to-patch interactions is well-reasoned and thoroughly ablated in the supplementary material.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across a wide variety of datasets and tasks (relative pose estimation, dense pointmap estimation, and scene-level camera tracking on Tanks & Temples) demonstrating substantial wall-clock speedups (up to ~4×) with negligible quality loss at moderate sparsity levels.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The core pooling-based block mask prediction and CDF/top-k thresholding closely resemble techniques from the LLM efficiency literature (such as SpargeAttention and SeerAttention), meaning the algorithmic contribution largely consists of adapting an existing paradigm to bidirectional vision tokens.

Under-exploitation of empirical insights: The analysis in Section 3.3 and Figure 5 demonstrates that middle layers are significantly more sensitive than early and late layers. However, the proposed method applies the same sparsity selection policy uniformly across layers rather than adapting the sparsity budget per layer according to depth.

Incomplete profiling of resource utilization: While latency speedups on an NVIDIA H100 are reported, the paper lacks detailed analysis of peak GPU memory (VRAM) savings and scaling behavior across different hardware architectures or varying block sizes $b$.

Noticeable quality cliff at high sparsity: As shown in Table 1 and Figure 7, when sparsity reaches ~75%, performance metrics drop substantially (e.g., RRA@5 drops from 73.4% to 46.0% on Tanks & Temples full sequences), indicating that the practical operating range is bounded around 25%–50% sparsity.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely bottleneck: feed-forward multi-view transformers (such as VGGT and pi^3) face quadratic memory and runtime complexity in their global attention layers, hindering scaling to long image sequences.

Insightful attention analysis: provides clear observations regarding the sparsity structure of cross-frame attention, identifying that attention mass is heavily localized on sparse geometric correspondences and concentrates primarily in the mid-layers of the aggregator.
Effective plug-and-play integration: the proposed method is training-free and requires no retraining or architecture modifications, making it easy to retrofit existing checkpoints.

Crucial domain-specific handling of special tokens: demonstrating that separating camera and register tokens from patch-level sparsification is critical to preventing accuracy collapse under high sparsity.
Extensive empirical benchmarking across multiple multi-view datasets (CO3Dv2, RealEstate10K, ScanNet, TUM, 7Scenes, NRGBD, DTU, ETH3D, and Tanks & Temples) with both VGGT and pi^3 backbones.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the core approach (predicting block masks via query/key average pooling followed by CDF/top-k filtering and executing block-sparse kernels) largely follows the formulations in recent LLM sparse attention works such as SpargeAttention and SeerAttention, with the primary adaptation being the separation of register/camera tokens.

Incomplete wall-clock runtime reporting on standard multi-view benchmarks: while Tanks & Temples shows significant speedup for large frame counts (100–200+ frames), many standard evaluations (e.g., DTU and ETH3D in Section 5.1) use only 10 frames per scene. The paper does not report whether block-sparse attention yields any wall-clock benefit over dense FlashAttention at small sequence lengths where kernel overhead can offset FLOP reductions.

Omission of critical hyperparameter details: the main text introduces block size b for average pooling and block-sparse kernels, but the specific choice of b (and whether it varies across image resolutions) is not clearly specified in Section 4.

Underutilization of the layer-importance findings: while Sections 3.3 and 3.4 show that aggregator mid-layers are substantially more sensitive than early/late layers (which can even be skipped), the method relies purely on per-layer dynamic CDF/top-k without investigating explicit layer-heterogeneous sparsity budgets or skipping outer layers to further improve speed.

strengths: Practical and timely problem: Addressing the quadratic computational complexity of global attention layers in recent feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction models (e.g., VGGT and π³) is an important and practically relevant challenge.

Insightful architectural analysis: The empirical analysis of global attention patterns provides clear insights, notably identifying that geometric correspondences concentrate primarily in mid-aggregator layers and that patch-to-patch interactions behave fundamentally differently from camera and register tokens.
Effective plug-and-play retrofit: The proposed method requires no backbone retraining or optimization, allowing immediate application to off-the-shelf pre-trained models.

Crucial domain-specific design: Decoupling special tokens (camera embeddings and registers) from the sparse patch-to-patch attention path is simple yet shown to be critical for preventing catastrophic performance degradation at higher sparsity.

Extensive empirical validation: The method is validated across a wide array of standard benchmarks (RealEstate10K, CO3Dv2, TUM, ScanNet, 7Scenes, NRGBD, DTU, ETH3D, and Tanks & Temples) across varying frame counts (up to 200+ frames) with wall-clock runtime measurements on modern hardware (NVIDIA H100).
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The underlying block-sparse formulation (average pooling Q/K followed by thresholded block mask selection) is heavily borrowed from existing sparse attention literature in LLMs (such as SpargeAttention and SeerAttention). The conceptual contribution beyond applying these techniques and isolating special tokens is modest.

Steep performance drops at high sparsity: While the paper advertises 'up to 4× faster inference', the empirical results show substantial drops in accuracy at high sparsity levels (e.g., in Table 1 on Tanks & Temples, RRA@5 drops from 83.9 to 57.1 at 75% sparsity for 200 frames). High accuracy is only retained at moderate sparsity ratios (25%–50%), corresponding to more modest real-world speedups (roughly 1.3× to 2.5× end-to-end).

Under-explored layer-adaptive budget: The analysis in Section 3 and Figure 5 clearly shows that middle aggregator layers are critical while early and late layers are largely insensitive to pruning/sparsity. However, the proposed method does not exploit this insight to allocate non-uniform, layer-dependent sparsity budgets or selectively bypass attention in non-critical layers.

Lack of comparison with competing acceleration strategies: The paper benchmarks against dense VGGT and non-sparse architectures, but does not compare against other standard acceleration baselines such as token downsampling/merging, cross-view epipolar/windowed attention, or linear attention variants.

strengths: Addresses a highly timely and critical bottleneck: recent feed-forward multi-view geometry transformers (such as VGGT, pi^3, and MapAnything) achieve state-of-the-art results but suffer from severe quadratic scaling bottlenecks in their global attention layers when processing large image sequences.

Provides valuable empirical insights into the attention dynamics of multi-view geometry transformers, specifically highlighting the cross-view geometric correspondence sparsity in patch tokens, the distinct behavior of special tokens (camera and register tokens), and the sensitivity differences across network depth (mid-layers being the most critical).

The method is training-free and plug-and-play, avoiding expensive re-training or fine-tuning while delivering tangible wall-clock speedups (up to 2x-3x end-to-end on long sequences up to 1000 frames on an H100 GPU).

Extensive empirical validation across three major architectures (VGGT, pi^3, MapAnything) and numerous standard benchmarks covering both relative camera pose estimation (CO3Dv2, RealEstate10K, TUM, ScanNet, Tanks & Temples) and multi-view 3D pointmap reconstruction (7Scenes, NRGBD, DTU, ETH3D).
Well-structured ablations validating core architectural decisions, such as preserving dense attention for special tokens and comparing training-free pooling versus learned projection layers.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is somewhat limited: the core block-sparse attention framework largely adapts existing concepts from recent LLM sparse attention literature (notably SpargeAttention and SeerAttention), using average-pooled Q/K similarity followed by combined top-k and CDF thresholding.

Missed opportunity on layer-adaptive sparsity: While Section 3 and the layer-skipping ablations demonstrate that mid-layers are substantially more critical and sensitive than early/late layers, the block selection hyperparameters (tau, rho) appear to be applied uniformly across all layers rather than dynamically allocating sparsity budgets conditioned on layer depth.

Runtime overhead breakdown of mask generation: While end-to-end speedups on long sequences are reported, the manuscript lacks a detailed latency breakdown of the overhead incurred by the low-resolution query/key pooling and thresholding relative to the block-sparse kernel execution on shorter sequences.

strengths: Addresses a pressing and practical bottleneck in recent state-of-the-art feed-forward 3D vision transformers (VGGT, π³, MapAnything), where quadratic global attention prevents scaling to long trajectories and large view sets.

Provides insightful empirical analysis of cross-view attention patterns, showing that global attention mass concentrates heavily on sparse geometric correspondences and peaks in the middle aggregator layers.

The domain-specific insight of separating special tokens (camera and register tokens) from patch tokens is simple yet crucial, preventing severe performance drops observed when naively applying generic sparse attention.
The approach is training-free and kernel-agnostic, avoiding costly model retraining while remaining robust across diverse models and sequence lengths.

Thorough empirical validation across three architectures and multiple standard benchmarks (ScanNet, Tanks & Temples, CO3Dv2, RealEstate10K, DTU, ETH3D, etc.), demonstrating up to 3× speedup on long sequences (up to 1000 frames) with negligible degradation in camera pose and 3D point estimation.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is somewhat incremental, as the core mechanism adapts and simplifies existing block-sparse attention strategies from LLMs (such as SpargeAttention and SeerAttention) rather than introducing a fundamentally new attention formulation.

The paper observes substantial differences in layer importance across depth (mid-layers being critical for VGGT), yet the proposed scheme applies uniform thresholding hyperparameters across all layers rather than exploring layer-adaptive sparsity budgets.
While latency speedups are documented, empirical peak GPU memory (VRAM) savings across long sequences (e.g., 100 to 1000 frames) are not systematically reported alongside the runtime plots.

strengths: Timely and practically significant problem: Feed-forward multi-view geometry foundation models (VGGT, π³, MapAnything) suffer from quadratic scaling in their global attention layers as sequence length grows. Providing an efficient inference solution for these models is highly valuable to the community.

Well-motivated empirical analysis: The paper provides clear observations regarding the structure of attention maps in geometry transformers, showing that cross-view attention concentrates along geometric correspondences and peaks in the middle aggregator layers.

Pragmatic, training-free design: The adaptation of block-sparse attention requires no fine-tuning or retraining of the underlying checkpoints. The specific architectural insight to treat special tokens (camera and register tokens) densely while sparsifying patch-to-patch attention is crucial and well-validated by ablations.

Extensive experimental evaluation: The authors evaluate across three modern architectures (VGGT, π³, MapAnything) across diverse benchmarks for both relative pose estimation and pointmap estimation (ScanNet, CO3D, TUM, RealEstate10K, ETH3D, DTU, 7Scenes, NRGBD, Tanks & Temples), including scaling tests up to 1000 frames.
weaknesses: Incremental methodological novelty: The core sparsification framework (average-pooling Q/K to build a coarse similarity matrix, selecting blocks via CDF and top-k thresholding, and calling a block-sparse kernel) is largely adapted from existing LLM sparse attention literature (e.g., SpargeAttention, SeerAttention). The novelty lies primarily in the application and the domain-specific handling of special tokens.

Disconnect between analysis and method execution: The paper emphasizes in Section 3 that the middle aggregator layers are substantially more critical and exhibit different attention behaviors than early/late layers. However, the proposed method applies a global CDF/top-k thresholding strategy across all layers rather than exploiting layer-dependent or adaptive sparsity budgets suggested by the analysis.

Missing operational parameters in the main text: Crucial hyperparameters, such as the exact block size b used for the block-sparse kernel during inference across the experiments, are not clearly detailed in Section 4 or Section 5 of the main manuscript.

Modest end-to-end acceleration on standard sequence lengths: While theoretical attention FLOP reduction is substantial and long-sequence (>300 frames) inference reaches ~2-3× speedup, for typical sequence lengths (<100 frames) the overall end-to-end speedup remains relatively modest due to the overhead of patchification, per-frame feature encoding, and dense task heads.
